title: Choose the homepage structure
question: The visual world is already LinCie's Station House. Choose how the single homepage lets a visitor arrive, orient, and wander.

options.label: The Open Platform
options.lineage: rural station arrival and maintained departure board
options.thesis: The homepage behaves like a real station arrival: welcome and identity sit on the platform, while the complete board is the first thing visitors can use.
options.viewport: A wide morning-sky opening places the welcome and software-engineering identity on the left, a large wood-toned board on the right, and a restrained station-house silhouette behind. Five equal departures pair poetic place names with literal on-page anchors; one small notice says the room is quiet for now. On phones, welcome comes first, then the board and three equal invitations to look, pause, or step inside.
options.topology: Arrival → complete board → same-page rooms → return platform footer; no route depends on motion or a hidden hotspot.
options.signatureInteraction: The board is a tactile-looking list of full anchor links. A current notice can open its honest detail in place, but the page remains fully useful without JavaScript.
options.responsive: The landscape simplifies into a stacked platform and board; route order and literal labels stay unchanged.
options.contentContract: Unavailable About, Projects, Offers, Thoughts, and Connect content appears as clearly labeled quiet rooms with useful next anchors, never invented filler.
options.risk: If the landscape dominates, the page becomes an illustration; the board must remain the highest-contrast, most useful object.

raised.raise: A single slim current-signal band beneath the welcome makes change visible without urgency, while the rest of the page stays achromatic and calm.
Every destination exposes the same named anatomy—place, literal label, state, and anchor—so the complete world can be scanned without decoding the scene.

options.label: The House Window
options.lineage: lived-in station house and threshold window
options.thesis: A visitor meets LinCie through a small lived-in room before choosing where to wander next.
options.viewport: A calm split opening pairs a concise identity note and one honest quiet-room signal with a station-house window scene. A continuous board rail sits beside and below it, giving all five on-page destinations equal weight without turning the page into a profile template.
options.topology: Person → visible board rail → same-page rooms → return to the station sign at the bottom.
options.signatureInteraction: The house window frames a nonessential current thought or comfort when supplied; when unavailable, it stays a labeled quiet notice rather than a fake detail.
options.responsive: The room and board become a single vertical reading order; the board moves before optional scene details.
options.contentContract: Personal facts remain limited to confirmed identity and trainee role; every missing room is explicit about being quiet for now.
options.risk: With little personal content available, the house can read like an empty profile card unless the board remains the dominant navigation object.

options.label: The Endpaper Map
options.lineage: picture-book endpaper and complete route index
options.thesis: The whole homepage is a gentle map: the station sits at the center, every destination is named, and wandering begins with certainty.
options.viewport: A large illustrated route map fills the opening with a clear station center, five labeled branch markers, and smaller forest, mountain, map, and lost-platform references kept subordinate. The welcome and trainee identity sit in a quiet paper panel beside the map; the current signal is a small posted note, not a badge.
options.topology: Station center → named same-page anchors → literal room sections → a footer map key and return-to-top control.
options.signatureInteraction: Selecting a labeled map marker moves to the corresponding on-page room and gives it a visible current-location cue; the full text list remains adjacent and works without the map.
options.responsive: The map becomes a compact stacked index above the rooms; no route depends on tracing a ribbon or reading a tiny marker.
options.contentContract: Every marker has a plain label and an honest state. Secondary destinations can be marked unavailable without pretending they are separate pages.
options.risk: A map can turn metaphor into decoding; literal labels and ordered text links must be co-equal with the illustration.

options.label: The Tending Shelf
options.lineage: kiln shelf with visible material stages
options.thesis: The homepage presents each destination as a tended object whose honest state is visible before anyone opens it.
options.viewport: The welcome sits above a long station shelf holding five labeled destinations. Each tag shows a plain label and one state—open, quiet, or growing—before the visitor reaches an on-page room; a single current note rests at the center rather than a ranking.
options.topology: Shelf tag → same-page room → visible state note → return to the shelf.
options.signatureInteraction: A tag can be selected to bring its room into focus, with the same state stated in text and never represented by color alone.
options.responsive: The shelf becomes a vertical list with full-width tags and no horizontal scroll.
options.case: Fuses cleanly with the Station House: it makes unavailable content and honest states legible, but it is less immediately personal than the open platform.
options.risk: State labels can drift into a project dashboard if the page treats every room as a status object.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A conventional personal portfolio homepage leads with a hero, a featured project, and a polished work grid.
canonCard.viewport: A large personal-brand headline and primary contact or explore action sit above one featured project, followed by a standard grid of work and a contact prompt.
canonCard.risk: It asks visitors to scan credentials before meeting the person or understanding the place.
